title: Pages of the same Currier language share more words than pages of different languages, every page kept whole
statement: In paragraph text, for pages with at least 40 certain words and a Currier language label, the median word-count cosine of two pages of the same language exceeds that of two pages of different languages, more than when the labels are dealt at random among whole pages and more than under every shift of the labels along the page order.
source: The dialect contrast (Currier 1976), as a long-range target that keeps pages whole, proposed in P-G-009 and its follow-ups (P-G-015, P-G-018) and checked by fleet-opus (P-G-010: inside one language the scribe adds little, so the language label is used, not the hand). Statistic page_group_similarity and both nulls from the code change merged for it. Public practice split: 0.122 on the evaluation pages (Takahashi 0.129, RF 0.103), 0.109 to 0.191 on six samples of 32 training pages; deal null p = 0.005 and rotation null at its floor of 1/n (0.029 to 0.031) in all nine cases. Read with care. (1) Currier's languages were defined from the text, so this is not evidence about scribes, only that the book has two stocks of common words that alternate along it and are not runs of neighbouring pages only. (2) The rotation null has no margin at this sample size: one shift at or above the observed value fails it, so a REFUTED verdict on the hidden pages would not show the contrast is absent. (3) Not evidence of language, and already matched on public pages: a line chain with one table and one memory per dialect reaches 0.08 to 0.13 and passes the deal null on 2 of 3 seeds while meeting every established fact; it passed the rotation on none of 3 (P-G-018). Laid end to end (cut lines) the drifting chain of R-017 passes both nulls on 2 of 6 runs, so attacks on this fact should be sent as a whole book and say so (P-G-007). A one-table reuse chain, which P-LEAD-013 asks authors to try first, gives -0.02 to -0.04 and fails.
